newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-NORMAN'S RESOLVE WHITTLED AWAY BY ROWDY GALLERY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NORMAN'S RESOLVE WHITTLED AWAY BY ROWDY GALLERY.

text.p: Greg Norman, golf's top- rated player and the central figure in more twists and turns of plot than your average soap opera star, tried on Tuesoay to calm the clamour raised by his latest weekend wobble.

Life in golf's fast lane has changed in the past 10 years, Norman said in his defence as he took time out from preparation for Thursday's first round of the U.S. Open at Congressional. Fans and other golf course folk take unjustified liberties, he said.

"The media coverage is so intense with not only print but television and video that people feel like they know you, and when they feel like they know you they feel like they can come up to you and say whatever they want to say, like you do to your buddy," he said.
The latest bit of damage control came after twin flare-ups from Norman at last week's Kemper Open at nearby Avenel.

A lame quip by the starter introducing Norman on Saturday at the Kemper Open alluded to U.S. President Bill Clinton's fall and knee injury at Norman's Hobe Sound home in Florida. Norman cast his most ferocious glare at the announcer and then pulled him into a nearby tent for a dressing down.
On Sunday, the charismatic Australian flamed up over what he thought was a derisive shout from the gallery.
Norman said he heard one thing, observers on hand heard something else. Reporters said Norman responded with an obscene gesture, which the Australian denies.

"Coming into the 17th hole last week, you've got to understand, there was a lot of emotion involved. I was still trying to give myself a chance of winning a golf tournament," said Norman, who finished tied for third.
Reporters at the scene thought they heard a shout of encouragement to the White Shark along the lines of, "There's chum in the water."
Norman, sensitive to last-round fiascoes following his fade from glory at last year's Masters, heard otherwise. "I heard the guy yell out from the gallery: 'Chunk it in the water.'"
Witnesses said the angered Australian made a crude hand gesture toward the fan, twice.

"I did not give him the bird," said Norman, referring to the upraised middle finger salute. "I can honestly say, I gestured to do it, but I did not give him the bird. So that is categorically untrue."

That answer sounded rather like a politician's denial from Norman, who Monday took his family to visit his presidential pal at the White House before announcing his purchase of a personal 737 Boeing jetliner and a multimillion-dollar deal to become an "ambassador" for Boeing.
Norman insisted his behaviour on the golf course is generally impeccable, especially considering the provocation he must endure.

"It's very difficult to control it all," he said. "I do a great job at it. I would like you guys to come and experience some of the things you hear out there. I mean, you too would be whittled away a little bit, too.

"It's not a lot of fun, especially when you're out there trying to be the person you want to be, trying to be the golfer you want to be, and try to uphold an image and respect for the game of golf that you love to play. It's very, very difficult.
"But again, it's whittle, whittle. A slow water torture test."
